This study examines the effectiveness of edge finite elements in approximating discrete maximum principles for a Poisson equation with Dirichlet boundary conditions. We explore various configurations of edge finite elements, both conforming and nonconforming, and investigate their ability to recover the best possible discrete analogue of the maximum principle. Our analysis emphasizes the role of element connectivity in achieving optimal results and demonstrates that edge finite elements can yield the best possible performance when employed in a complete-element approach. However, this achievement comes at the cost of robustness when incorporating nonconforming elements, as demonstrated by specific examples.

This paper delves into the properties of a specific vertex operator algebra, created through the parafermion construction, which is derived from the affine Lie superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$. We establish generators for this vertex operator algebra and outline its extended symmetry, which results in a classification of highest weight modules. Additionally, we explore the implications of this classification for the parafermion vertex operator algebra when $osp(1|2n)$ is replaced by $osp(2|2n)$.

We introduce a novel perspective on training a student model that leverages
saliency-based methods to identify and prioritize the knowledge being transferred
from a more experienced teacher model. Unlike conventional approaches, our
methodology bypasses the need to estimate explicit uncertainty or posterior
distributions in the teacher model. Instead, we employ a saliency-based approach
to identify and amplify the key features in the teacher that contribute to the
classification decisions. Our proposed framework consists of two primary modules:
a saliency-generating network and a feature-enhancing encoder. The former uses
backpropagation to determine the feature importance in the teacher model, while
the latter amplifies these salient features to create a more pronounced pattern
that the student model can learn from. We integrate our approach into a
knowledge amalgamation framework and demonstrate through comprehensive experiments
on three different datasets that our method achieves highly competitive performance
while requiring substantially fewer iterations. Additionally, our method yields
notably improved results when incorporating additional natural variations in the
teacher model, indicating an significant advantage in terms of robustness.

Previous research suggested that a self-organizing grid cell model effectively captures the brain's underlying spatial coding, with cells contributing to a hexagonal map of an environment through robust, locally consistent neighboring connections. However, in reality, animals' internal representations of space are significantly shaped by external sensory inputs and visual cues. In this study, we investigate ways to make the grid cell model more responsive to such environmental cues. We began by incorporating local sensory-driven currents into the standard self-organizing grid cell model, with the goal of observing how the grid cell pattern adapts in response to these influences. Our results reveal that when we included local currents with sufficiently wide spatial extent and moderate to high gain, the grid cell pattern transitioned from an orderly hexagonal structure to a distorted arrangement reflecting the shape of nearby sensory features. Moreover, when we positioned a prominent visual cue, like a salient object, within the environment, we found that the corresponding parts of the grid cell map became notably more ordered, with cells nearby exhibiting greater responsiveness to local currents and more defined boundaries. These findings suggest that higher-level spatial perception and navigation may rely on an interactive network of self-organizing grid cell modules, with each module's grid cell map influenced by local sensory currents and external environmental cues.

The global magnetic fields in Jupiter, Saturn, and various other gas giant planets remain somewhat of a mystery. Recent research suggests that these planetary magnetic fields may be influenced by a kinematic dynamo driven by their rapid rotation rates and the interaction between their atmospheric hydrogen layers and slowly conducting helium cores. This concept needs further exploration, although the condition $D^2 \ll 1$ restricts the applicability of the resistive magnetohydrodynamic model used by research. This study substitutes a more accurate numerical approach and utilizes higher-order finite differences to examine the effects of rotational instability on kinematic dynamos in planetary loops. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the traditional solar dynamo theory still provides valuable insights and that the cyclic behavior in research simulations is maintained even at extremely low rotation rates characteristic of the Earth. The research also reveals that the Earth's magnetic field generation pattern may be significantly different from research's standard assumption. The findings also indicate that the Earth's magnetic field generation pattern may be significantly different from research's standard assumption. The research also reveals that kinematic dynamos have a tendency to produce multiple stable equilibriums and that nonlinear interactions can result in solar-type cycles in research simulations. The research also reveals that kinematic dynamos have a tendency to produce multiple stable equilibriums and that nonlinear interactions can result in research simulations producing magnetic configurations similar to research's standard assumption.

We establish an initial count of four distinct S4 quartic extensions in the rational number field that meet a specific condition, where it's predicted that a vast majority of elliptic curves from the curve families of Rankin--Silverman and Kato--Katsura will not gain rank one, except in a limited number of cases when the field extension has a specific transfer of ramified primes. Building on this finding, we make the broader assertion that there should be fewer than twenty-five different S4 quartic extensions in the rational number field that meet this desired condition, where it's predicted that a vast majority of elliptic curves from these two families will not gain rank one, except in a limited number of cases when the field extension has a certain transfer of ramified primes.

We investigate the time-dependent density-density correlation function for a system undergoing an arbitrary quadratic quench from an initial steady-state condition. In particular, we analyze the full expression for the heat and entropy production associated with a specific quench, where we demonstrate that the entropy change can be divided into two components following the quench. In certain cases, we observe that the full entropy shift can be captured by the heat production divided by the square of the temperature. Additionally, we find that certain discrete quantum quenches result in periodic revivals of both correlation functions and scattering probabilities, suggesting that smooth quenoses can be created by introducing linear terms. Our study utilizes a Lagrange multiplier approach that enables the determination of relevant and irrelevant modes during the quench, further allowing us to examine the entropy production in relation to the temperature and entropy changes.

We investigate the time evolution of the superoperator Yang-Baxter equation (SYBE) solution in a combined system and environment, using a simple example based on the Ising model. Our analysis employs the matrix product operator (MPO) representation of the superoperator, and we find that its time-twisted state is exactly solvable for a specific interaction time. We propose that this time-twisted state can be used as a non-unitary state that reaches maximum distinguishability at a certain time, and this time is equivalent to the minimal time required to distinguish between two non-unitary states in quantum non-unitary dynamics. We also examine the convergence of the MPO representation in a combined system and environment, and we find that its twist time can be used as an indicator of when the MPO representation converges quickly enough to be useful for calculating thermal states using the time-evolution method.

We investigate the existence of a nondegenerate regular simplex within the unit cube $Q_n$ with interpolation nodes. Specifically, we determine the minimum number of interpolation nodes required to ensure the existence of such a simplex, and we characterize the configuration of nodes that achieves this minimum. Our analysis leverages the concept of an $n$-simplex, whose facets can be used to analyze the stability of the regular simplex, and we apply the Ky Fan theorem to draw conclusions about the existence of the desired simplex.

We examined the surface conduction of two types of silicon interfaces: etched silicon and silicon etched with buffer oxide. Using gate strips, we found that carrier concentrations in etched silicon and silicon etched with buffer oxide are $1.0\times 10^{11}$ and $8.0\times 10^{10}$ per cubic centimeter, respectively. As a result, we discovered a higher $I_D$ current in etched silicon than in silicon etched with buffer oxide due to increased carrier concentration. Additionally, we found that etched oxide can be as thick as 100 ${\rm \AA}$ without significantly affecting surface conduction. However, we observed a significant decrease in $I_D$ when oxide thickness exceeds 100 ${\rm \AA}$. A 5-nm tunneling oxide thickness was assumed in our analysis.

This paper develops the twisted homotopy K-theory of cdh descent and Milnor excision forms found in [6] and [7]. We incorporate these descriptors into the definition of twisted homotopy K-theory, denoting it as $KH_{\mathfrak{d},\mathfrak{m}}(X)$. We then investigate $KH_{\mathfrak{d},\mathfrak{m}}(X)$ for local ring spectra $X$ associated with local Noetherian rings $A$. By examining the relationship between $KH_{\mathfrak{d},\mathfrak{m}}(X)$ and the cdh and henselian twisted homotopy K-theory of the residue field of $A$, we determine the additivity and excision properties of $KH_{\mathfrak{d},\mathfrak{m}}(X)$. Furthermore, we establish an equivalence between $KH_{\mathfrak{d},\mathfrak{m}}(X)$ and the twisted étale homotopy K-theory of $X$, leading to an explicit calculation of $KH_{\mathfrak{d},\mathfrak{m}}(X)$.

The evolution of a planet's atmosphere, whether it's a terrestrial or gaseous world, is greatly impacted by the interconnection between its interior and exterior layers. The water vapor-silicate rock interaction inside planets, for example, can influence their atmospheres through processes like crust recycling, core-mantle interactions, and volcanic activity. These connections can create cycling patterns that affect the atmosphere over time and may result in enduring effects such as atmospheric retention or loss. In our research, we explore how these interior-atmospheric cycling interactions affect exoplanet atmospheres through processes like gas giant contraction, steam jet delivery of oxygen to dense rocky cores, and volcanic oxygen and carbon dioxide release in mini-Neptunes. These processes, although sometimes brief, can significantly shape the atmospheres of these planets and ultimately lay the groundwork for more intricate processes like atmospheric chemistry and gas exchange between planets and their host stars. In the future, we anticipate that studies integrating planetary interior models with atmospheric simulations will provide further insights into how these cycling patterns affect atmospheres over time.

In a previous study, a unique methyl cation production pattern around 1,2-propanediol (1,2-PDO) was noted, differing from 1,3-PDO's typical methyl cation distribution. This work investigates the 1,2-PDO structure to understand this anomaly. Using density functional theory, we examine 1,2-PDO in its gas phase and solvated in water, simulating its conformation through O-H bond stretching. Our results indicate that the molecule maintains a cyclic form and avoids opening up into a linear structure, even when simulating methyl cation formation. A comparison of optimized 1,2-PDO and 1,3-PDO structures shows that the latter can transition between cyclic and linear forms, which is essential for explaining the differing methyl cation distributions observed in mass spectrometry experiments.

Quantum circuit simulations offer a promising route to efficiently evaluating tensor network states and their dynamics. However, most tensor networks require a full unitary parametrization of the circuit, making them less suited for simulations employing limited unitary rotations. We introduce an efficient method for approximating matrix products with quantum circuits, allowing for flexible parametrization. This approach leverages a novel variation of the matrix product operator variational algorithm, utilizing a unique decomposition that facilitates seamless integration with quantum simulation workflows. Notably, this method enables the direct incorporation of existing tensor networks generated by other techniques, such as time-dependent density functional theories. Our proposed algorithm boasts a significant reduction in the number of required quantum circuit parameters while maintaining superior accuracy. This is achieved without the need for additional optimization beyond the initial parametrization. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method with a range of simulations, including systems involving multiple valence electrons and coupled spin chains. The code implementing our algorithm is freely accessible as an open-source project PyMPAO.

The classification of tumor tissues is a critical aspect of cancer diagnosis, treatment planning, and research. Recent studies utilizing graph neural networks have shown significant improvements in labeling tumor tissues based on genetic expression data and corresponding information about cell compositions, known as the molecular cell composition (MCC). However, existing solutions rely on manually extracted features and assumed structures, which limits their potential when applied to other domains. In response, we developed a novel framework called DeepMCCPredictor, which leverages graph neural networks to directly classify tumor tissues represented as graphs, also known as proteomic landscapes. By processing proteomic data with minimal preprocessing, our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods, according to evaluations conducted using four diverse tumor tissue datasets.

This research paper introduces a new type of nonlinear Hawkes process that can handle multiple interactions between various events in different event streams. We've developed an innovative R Shiny application, allowing users to visually explore and analyze data generated by our nonlinear Hawkes process model. Notably, the implementation includes an significant adjustment to the standard nonlinear Hawkes model, enabling the simulation of bimodal distributions that were previously unachievable. Additionally, we've incorporated several features that demonstrate the Hawkes process model's ability to effectively capture interaction phenomena, including: (1) learning the absolute and relative scales of different event streams; (2) identifying instances where two events in the same stream influence each other, while also describing complex relationships between events in different streams.

We've introduced an open-source, flexible code called Nyx-gpuFMM for simulating large scales of the universe on supercomputers. Nyx-gpuFMM utilizes the Fast Multipole Method (FMM) to speed up computationally intensive gravity calculations, which would otherwise slow down the code. By leveraging the FMM algorithm, Nyx-gpuFMM can quickly determine the gravitational influence of distant particles and accurately calculate the effects of nearby particles. This strategic pairing of FMM and Nyx-gpuFMM allows it to efficiently manage vast numbers of astrophysical particles in simulations.

We address the complicated issue of adapting cross-anatomy domain adaptation to segment different human body regions with limited labeled data. Our proposed method, Contrastive Semi-supervised learning for Cross-Anatomy Domain Adaptation (CS-CADA), leverages semi-supervised learning techniques and contrastive learning to overcome existing challenges. CS-CADA employs a multi-domain framework that incorporates unsupervised cross-domain learning and semi-supervised learning within each domain. This framework enables the exploration of novel low-dimensional features that are both domain-invariant and distinctive. By applying self-supervised optimization to adapt boundaries and reweight cross-domain samples, CS-CADA enhances segmentation performance. Our method demonstrates superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods for adapting brain and abdominal organ segmentation, achieving a significant gain of 6.3% in the BrainS seg. metric and 8.3% in the AdS seg. metric. Additionally, CS-CADA successfully demonstrated robust performance on newly acquired data, showcasing little overfitting (-0.8% in the BrainS seg. metric and -2.3% in the AdS seg. metric) when compared to our results on in-domain data.

We provide an evaluation of the long-standing issue of four-dimensional supersymmetric gravity being impossible to fully comprehend in a four-dimensional context.  By examining the behavior of BRS symmetry in supergravity, we find that it can, in fact, be properly understood when viewed as a five-dimensional theory.  To support this, we show that the BRS algebra in a four-dimensional context includes an unwanted anti-commutative term, which vanishes in a five-dimensional context due to being proportional to the extra dimension's fifth component.  We then demonstrate that this extra dimension can be made inconsequential by imposing suitable infinitesimal restrictions on the four-dimensional context.  As a result, we are able to derive a five-dimensional interpretation of BRS symmetry in supergravity, which helps confirm the existence of a auxiliary five-dimensional metric field previously proposed in the context of BRS symmetry in supergravity.  Furthermore, we propose that this field has the ability to explain why Calabi-Yau manifolds are able to withstand the effects of a large negative cosmological constant.

In high-density plasma devices like HIBP at the PSI, a plasma waveplate is utilized for converting circularly polarized microwave photons to linearly polarized ones, enabling access to electron density information through Thomson scattering. The optimal functionality of this technology relies heavily on the presence of a specific magnetic field that is used to create and control long-lived plasma waves within the experimental area. Nevertheless, achieving sufficient wave propagation length becomes increasingly difficult as electron density rises with growing power input. A theoretical model of plasma wave propagation has been developed to better comprehend the relationship between necessary thickness and the opposing absorption effects. Based on this understanding, it was determined that a thicker waveplate with effective photoconversion would require unusually high power levels, likely exceeding the limitations of the HIBP facility. A possible alternative considered is the use of a thinner waveplate with an optimized plasma geometry that could potentially provide comparable results while using significantly lower electron densities. A numerical simulation indicates that such a setup would indeed yield sufficient photoconversion even with shorter propagation lengths. The conditions necessary for efficient waveplate functionality have been determined and are influenced by both magnetic field strength and minimum electron density.

We examine the electric dipole moment of the tau lepton within a specialized version of the two-Higgs doublet model, known as the type-II 2HDM. This variant incorporates the maximal mixing hypothesis commonly seen in this model framework. Our analysis reveals that the primary contribution to the tau electric dipole moment arises from the exchange of a light pseudoscalar Higgs particle. As a result, we establish a crucial connection between the predicted values of this electric dipole moment and the mass difference between the pseudoscalar and scalar Higgs particles. Given that existing experiments have already provided some insight into this Higgs sector, we are able to establish a minimum value for the tau electric dipole moment at approximately $10^{-18}$ e.cm. However, if we assume that a forthcoming experiment can accurately measure this value, we propose that it could serve as a reliable indicator of the mass spectrum within the 2HDM. Consequently, if the predicted mass patterns associated with certain CP-violating phases can be replicated, we propose that the forthcoming experiment for the tau electric dipole moment be carried out with a level of precision at least 100 times more refined.

High-rate code construction via rank metric is achieved using a specific construction method based on polynomial properties. A newly proposed evaluation matrix construction allows for the creation of rank metric codes with high error correction capabilities, particularly for rates greater than 1/2. Existing rank metric code types, such as Generalized Minimum Rank Codes and a specific variant of Gabidulin codes, already exist but only provide limited error correction up to rank $r \leq \frac{p^m-1}{2}$ due to their rank-distance natures. In contrast, this work's invented codes offer enhanced error correction capabilities, surpassing this limitation, when used in conjunction with a specific decoding algorithm, particularly when $p>2$. Furthermore, this new code type relates to both GMRC and EGMC, exhibiting distinct characteristics that distinguish it from these code types, including unique properties and performance in scenarios with high-rank errors.

The structure of conformal block expansions for geodesic operators in two-dimensional AdS space of varying dimensions can be used to test the consistency of dual conformal field theories, and this test holds regardless of whether the geodesic intersects the conformal boundary. However, previous analyses in AdS$_{d+1}$ for $d\neq 2$ found that the conformal block expansion of a geodesic operator whose trajectory does not intersect the boundary is comprised of conserved current blocks that can be expressed in terms of AdS$_{d}$ geodesic operators when $d\neq 2$. Contrary to this, our study reveals that in AdS$_{2}$, the same type of block that arises in the expansion of a non-boundary intersecting geodesic operator in AdS$_{2}$ actually corresponds to the block of a different conformal representation and can be linked to the dual conformal field theory via a different method, involving the use of Chern-Simons-like variables and a change of variables that relates them to AdS$_{3}$ geodesic operators whose trajectory does intersect the boundary.

We employed two neural network approaches, a physics-informed neural network and a deep convolutional neural network, to analyze their effectiveness in estimating weak gravitational lensing effects using simulated data. The results showed that the neural networks can recover the lensing effects with high accuracy and with less noise present in the data. We found that the neural networks outperformed traditional methods, specifically the HalloDark estimator. We also observed that using multiple views of the same field of view led to more precise estimations of the lensing effects. Ultimately, we found that the neural networks have great potential for accurately estimating the lensing effects and could potentially be used for real data.

In 2006, Gelfand and MacPherson defined combinatorial differential manifolds as a part of their broader work on combinatorial versions of various geometric concepts. Their framework specifically focused on differentiable manifolds, with an aim to incorporate the principles of differential topology. Building upon this foundation, we have been exploring ways to generalize Gelfand and MacPherson's idea to the context of smooth varieties, with varieties serving as an equivalent framework to differentiable manifolds. Our work ultimately seeks to establish a parallel theory, where the role of smooth varieties is analogous to that of combinatorial differential manifolds in relation to their topological counterparts. In this particular study, we have created a dictionary that enables the seamless translation between the two frameworks, thereby demonstrating their profound connection. As a result, this relationship now allows us to bypass the intricacies of combinatorial differential topology and instead tackle its related problems via the methods applicable to smooth varieties, with this proof-in-principle being exemplified through its successful application to a problem initially posed by Gelfand and MacPherson themselves.

The Type II supernova SN~2020jfo was closely observed and its spectroscopic analysis revealed a high ratio of nickel to iron in its emitted spectra, significantly exceeding typical values and surpassing even the ratios found in the sun. This exceptional ratio is attributed to a short-lived gas layer in the SN's surrounding, with an estimated age of around half an month, where numerous elements including heavy ones were rapidly formed due to the intense release of energy from the supernova's explosion. A comparison with theoretical predictions from SN simulations showed that a dense, compact and short-lived outer layer in SN~2020jfo could explain both the unusual ratios of nickel to iron as well as other observations like its broad spectral lines and intense light absorption, offering a distinctive insight into the complex structures of SN and the phenomena of gamma-ray bursts.

A unique lobster-eye optics system is used in the MIMOS-2 instrument to focus solar radiation. This system consists of two distinct image streams: a cross-like shape and a concentric one. Previously, only the concentric images were utilized to calculate the solar distance. Recently, obtained data feature both types of images. A rotation-variant cross-like projection model was developed to analyze these new data. The model incorporates an azimuthal rotation angle, which was initially unknown. By incorporating additional constraints, a parameter estimation technique was able to determine the optical system's parameters. It was discovered that the azimuthal rotation angle has a direct correlation with the angle of the cross-like image, which indicates a specific segment of the optics system. Additionally, the rotation-variant model enabled a more accurate calculation of the solar distance, which was found to be 0.98 AU during the 2018 campaign. This new model also demonstrated its effectiveness in predicting data values for both types of images.

We employ level set methods in conjunction with techniques from viscosity solutions and degenerate elliptic equations to analyze second-order fully nonlinear PDEs, specifically equations of the form $F(x,u,Du,D^2u)=0$. We introduce a level set formulation for these equations and establish a formal derivation leading to a Hamilton-Jacobi equation. Ultimately, our findings justify the use of level set formulations as a means of resolving uniqueness issues and multiple solution patterns for the original PDE.

To streamline halo finding and enhance the efficiency of subsequent N-body simulations, we propose a method where a single simulation is used to predict halo masses based on an initial density field. Instead of tracking multiple simulations to determine the most likely halo mass, this approach utilizes a statistical model that estimates halo masses from a single simulation's density field. However, incorporating a density-only model into the analysis incurs an accuracy cost, particularly for regions with high halo number density. In-depth calculations reveal that a density-only model results in an average error of ~0.77(1.12) times the standard halo mass when subjected to an elevated (~1.59) amplitude of initial scalar perturbations. Furthermore, we observed that using a density-only model leads to over/underestimation of halo masses in ~50%/48% of cases. To enhance the efficiency of this approach, we explored integrating the radial density profile of nearby halos into the statistical model. While incorporating the density profiles of surrounding halos reduces the average error to ~0.85(1.26) times the standard halo mass, it also complicates the simulation by introducing additional variables. In order to maintain the simplicity required for future N-body simulations, we opted against this modification. In order to facilitate the straightforward implementation of this algorithm into existing codes, we also developed a parallel version of the algorithm. Nevertheless, our experiments indicate that the proposed method achieves comparable performance to traditional methods to the extent that performance differences are negligible for realistic halo

In this study, a semi-supervised version of the Convolutional Neural Matrix Factorization (CNMF) method was developed and tested on piano transcription. CNMF, a hybrid technique combining CNMF and supervised Nonnegative Matrix Factorization (NMF), was evaluated in a piano transcription context with fewer labeled notes. Our experiments demonstrated that semi-supervised CNMF (ssCNMF) surpasses leading low-rank factorization methods along with supervised deep learning approaches, specifically Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Transposed CNN (TransCNN). Specifically, ssCNMF achieved more accurate piano transcription compared to CNMF, NMF, CNN, and TransCNN when presented with limited labeled data. Additionally, ssCNMF was found to excel in piano transcription when presented with fewer labeled notes, demonstrating the potential for improved piano transcription with less required human annotation.

This research introduces a novel approach to assigning properties like mass, specific angular momentum, and energy to individual fluid elements within stars that rotate. Unlike conventional methods, this approach bypasses the utilization of one-dimensional circulation streams, instead directly determining the characteristics of these elements via an overlying potential field. A comprehensive analysis of the resulting mass, angular momentum, and energy profiles has been conducted for rotating stars across a broad spectrum of eccentricity levels. The resulting mass profiles have been found to be exceptionally accurate, with minimal deviations of less than a percent in comparison to established models. Similarly, the predicted angular momentum profiles demonstrate precision, with an overall accuracy of better than three percent. However, the calculation of energy profiles reveals an average error of approximately fifteen percent. A key finding indicates that the one-dimensional circulation streams have a minimal influence on the mass and angular momentum distribution within the star, with only a minor impact on the overall energy profile.

A technique known as selective labeling seeks to minimize the cost of obtaining labeled data for the purpose of machine learning. It does this by identifying a limited subset of existing, unlabeled data that, when labeled, would be highly beneficial in enhancing the performance of machine learning models. Selective labeling can be particularly useful in expensive or difficult-to-obtain labeling processes, such as those requiring human judgment or intervention. The benefit of selective labeling becomes even more apparent in real-world applications where there is a vast amount of unlabeled data available. It is interesting to note that the problem of selecting the most effective subset of unlabeled data for labeling to improve machine learning performance is computationally complex, belonging to the NP-hard class. In response, this paper introduces an innovative method based on the kernel ordinal regression model that efficiently determines the most beneficial subset of unlabeled data for labeling. In comparison to existing methods, our proposed approach produces a much more accurate result while requiring significantly less computational time. Moreover, we demonstrate the superiority of our method over the state of the art through a series of rigorous experiments conducted on various datasets in both supervised and semi-supervised scenarios.

The merger of two neutron stars or a neutron star and a black hole's merger produces neutron stars that emit electromagnetic and gravitational waves. Although we can infer information about these mergers from both types of radiation, combining their simultaneous observation provides more detailed insights. Future experiments with advanced gravitational wave detectors and highly sensitive telescopes will allow for the in-depth analysis of neutron star coalescence events, significantly improving our understanding of these events. This study examines how precisely we can measure neutron star properties, astrophysical parameters, and heavy element creation in future high-end observations of neutron star mergers, also considering how the advanced detectors' improvements can significantly enhance our knowledge in this field.

The understanding of social determinants of health can benefit from mining clinical notes, which are rich in informative details about patients' lifestyles, living conditions, and life events beyond standardized clinical data. Although machine learning models can effectively identify relevant sections of clinical notes, a crucial step is often overlooked in the existing research - the lack of standard labels and structured formats for organizing extracted information. In this research, we tackle this challenge by introducing a novel approach that combines automatic section detection with hierarchical clustering to create meaningful categories for organizing clinical notes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to two diverse datasets of clinical notes, which show that our approach yields a high degree of accuracy in both detecting relevant sections and creating structured categories for organizing extracted information. Moreover, our technique allows for the incorporation of domain-specific expertise in the form of hierarchical labels, which serves as a guide for mapping extracted information to intended categories. We have made our code and datasets available for further research in this area.

We've developed a new model that enables the discontinuous dynamics of a swimmer switching between two states corresponds to the dynamics described by an index-2 switching map. We've used this new framework to find the smallest number of switches required to move the swimmer from an initial position to a target position, and have analyzed how this number varies as the frequency of switching increases in models that simulate laminar and turbulent fluid dynamics. In particular, we've investigated how this number is affected by the frequency of switching in relation to the natural timescales of the dynamical systems at the two endpoints, and have compared our results to predictions made by other researchers.

Our analysis of bookings and community activity at an independent venue in Manchester, UK, spanning almost a decade, reveals how the pandemic's abrupt closure in March 2020 significantly reduced diversity in urban social interactions and community resilience. Following the initial lockdown, there was a gradual, uneven increase in bookings driven by limited, cautious engagement. As COVID-19 restrictions eased, an uptick in bookings accelerated before slowing during the Russian-Ukrainian conflict and subsequent recession. In contrast to previous fluctuations, this time around diversity declined in response. In contrast to previous instances of growth, this time around resilience, as measured by the ability of communities to reconfigure and adapt, was evident only in the long term. A marked reduction in niche specialization, accompanied by an increase in bookings for established groups, characterized this period. It wasn't until the outbreak of the SARS-CoV-2 omicron variant in 2021, leading to renewed restrictions, that diversity began to rebound. This research provides an empirical framework for understanding the complex, high-dimensional dynamics underlying urban community dynamics and suggests that while certain events may seem fleeting, their consequences can have lasting effects, ultimately shaping the future of these communities.

The massive young star V1057 Cygni has an unstable and dynamic disc surrounding it. Despite being located in the Orion Nebula, this star and its disc are significantly more massive than the average. Researchers have studied the evolution of V1057 Cygni's disc using the ESPRISE and SEEDS observations, and their analysis revealed that a migrating object in the disc is responsible for the instability. A team of scientists simulated the dynamics of the inner disc, considering the effects of gravitational influence and particle collisions, and their model matched the observations from SEEDS and ESPRISE. However, the results also indicated that a large amount of dust was being removed from the inner disc. To verify this finding, a second simulation was conducted using the GULLY model to compare the distributions of removing dust grains with mass less than 10^-8 solar masses in the inner disc. The simulation showed that a significant proportion of small dust grains was being ejected from the inner disc, and this removal mechanism could be linked to the presence of an outflow system in V1057 Cygni.

Intuitively, a scattering theory can be understood through its asymptotic algebra and scattering matrix, which remain consistent under small perturbations. This paper develops a rigorous framework for this concept, based on geometric scattering theories. It first explores general conditions for the asymptotic algebra and scattering matrix to remain unchanged, and then delves into specific scenarios, examining how these conditions apply to free scattering, Schr\"{o}dinger scattering, and Dirac scattering under various types of nearsightened observability and completeness.

As the 5G era unfolds, there's growing public concern regarding 5G's potential impact on health, mirroring the cautious approach adopted with pre-5G technology in the 1990s. To accurately assess 5G's exposure, a detailed understanding of how radio signals behave around cellular towers is necessary. Unfortunately, health-focused research on 5G typically overlooks this aspect by relying on general 5G characteristics. In contrast, this study takes a novel approach by integrating international exposure guidelines with building attenuation patterns to estimate the exposure levels from 5G and previous technologies. The analysis reveals that 5G's exposure, especially when considering the effects of building attenuation, can exceed previous levels, particularly in offices and semi-outdoor environments, and cautions that a one-size-fits-all approach to 5G exposure assessment is inadequate.

This report outlines a novel approach to determining the surface of ocean waves, based on an analysis of the wave's envelope. The proposed method involves transforming the problem into a fourth-order partial differential equation, with a known integral relationship between the surface and envelope. To solve this equation, an iterative technique is employed, utilizing a series of approximations derived from the Laplace transformation of the envelope. The resulting algorithm surfaces-reconstructs the ocean wave profile.

The surface layer theorem originally established by Iglesias and Michor determines the local structure of differential forms on finite-dimensional manifold maps. We have expanded this research to consider infinite-dimensional manifold maps within the context of locally convex spaces. Additionally, our findings include the introduction of an explicit algorithm for determining the local structure of differential forms and a proof of the surface layer theorem for closed mappings.

This paper introduces an advanced management system for a hierarchical layer structure, in which multiple modules work together to overcome obstacles in a dark environment using sonar sensors. The developers of the system created a series of computer simulations and thoroughly tested its key features. In the process, they gathered valuable new data that led to several key improvements, including a significant enhancement to the navigation performance and a layer-based control approach with improved localization capabilities.

The impact of contextual information on the effectiveness of deep learning models in identifying fake news has been a subject of research and debate. To provide a clear conclusion, our study re-examines and expands upon existing analysis by incorporating new context-aware models and evaluating them with previously unused data. Our findings demonstrate that context is, in fact, highly beneficial in enhancing the performance of these models, which can now achieve over 90% accuracy in detecting false information according to the F-score metric. Our research also reveals that model performance is highly sensitive to the quality of underlying news datasets and suggests several avenues for future investigation in this field.

A theoretical model is developed to investigate transport phenomena in semiconductor superlattices subjected to a unidirectional electric field, focusing on a two-dimensional space with a one-dimensional barrier. The proposed system demonstrates a unique entropy-based measure of a nonequilibrium thermodynamic state that remains constant, as predicted by the nonequilibrium statistical thermodynamics theory. The structure's entropy is found to be directly proportional to the square of the thermal flux and is influenced by an electric current that induces a nonequilibrium chemical potential in the absence of temperature gradients. A nonequilibrium electrochemical potential profile results in a hysteresis effect in the system's phase diagram. The curvature of the superlattice affects the thermal flux, nonequilibrium chemical potential, and hysteresis, and it is compared to experimental data. The model also reveals that the system's entropy and hysteresis are interconnected, and it identifies the nonequilibrium thermodynamic states that give rise to hysteresis and oscillatory behavior.

Our research offers a suboptimal policy for selecting the decoding order that achieves nearly optimal security performance while significantly reducing the computational burden. By analyzing the exponential growth of possible decoding orders, we develop an approximate optimal strategy and demonstrate that even a random ordering follows a similar distribution shape. Based on this insight, we derive a simplified threshold-based rule for determining whether to generate a new decoding order or stick with an existing one, depending on the current security level and the computational burden. This approach allows us to determine the optimal parameters that balance security and computational efficiency. We examine the trade-off between these factors and explore the resulting performance metrics. We also convey the suboptimal policy in a compact and clear code that can be readily implemented.

We introduce a novel method for solving a problem called L1-PCA, which involves reducing data from high-dimensional spaces to a lower dimensional space while minimizing the mean squared error between data points and identifying the principal components. This approach is applicable to datasets presented in the spherical domain. However, our method goes beyond standard techniques in two key ways. Firstly, it maintains the rotational invariance property when determining the principal components. Secondly, it uses a non-smooth penalty function to regulate the dimensionality reduction. To compute the principal components, our method solves a two-block optimisation problem which includes a smooth data fitting component and a non-smooth component representing the invariance property. To solve this problem, we developed an iterative algorithm which alternates between solving a smooth eigenvalue problem and taking the spectral norm of a matrix. Notably, the algorithm can take advantage of parallel computing to speed up processing large datasets. Additionally, our method provides an estimate of the optimal dimensionality for the reduced data space. To evaluate our method, it performed several times faster than existing techniques and produced similar or better results on a range of benchmark datasets.

We propose a method to validate annotated data by leveraging paraphrasing techniques to detect label inconsistencies.  A set of paraphrasing models is trained on a given annotation set and used to generate alternative labels for the same data points.  Labels that differ from the original annotations indicate potential annotation errors, while consistent labels provide validation for the original annotations.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in both unsupervised and semi-supervised settings for validaton of annotated datasets.

We address the complexity of assessing whether a given half-positional game situation can be broken down into independent prefix-based situations that lead to a winning condition. Our main findings involve both an affirmative proof for a specific class of games and a counterexample indicating that for another class, such a decomposition might not always exist, even when combined with certain allowing strategies. Additionally, we demonstrate that certain supergames over infinite sequences possess non-half-positional winning conditions, whereas others require independent prefix-based situations for analysis.

X-ray spectra from the High Energy Stereoscopic System on the Isaac Newton Telescope and the Soft X-ray telescope on the Yohkoh satellite for the asynchronous polar V723 Mon during its 2020 outburst, allow the identification of highly variable absorption features and edge-like structures, which are at odds with the low-variable soft X-ray spectra from the standard polar PV Cephei during its 2011 outburst. Asynchronous and standard polar spectra exhibit distinct differences in their geometry, with asynchronous poles featuring colliding streams covering a larger percentage of the accretion region, resulting in more pronounced and variable X-ray spectra. The comparison of V723 Mon's X-ray light curve to that of the standard polar PV Cephei during their respective outbursts reveals a difference in their peak patterns, with V723 Mon displaying a double-hump shape and a delayed secondary peak compared to the single-hump light curve of PV Cephei. The variation in X-ray spectra and light curves between asynchronous and standard poles can provide a diagnostic tool for determining the subclass of a given polar system.

A combined fluid-structure interaction (FSI) analysis involves solving two distinct problems: the motion of an elastic structure influencing nearby fluid dynamics, and the flow affecting the same underlying structure. To tackle this challenge, a method divides the computation into two parts, solving the structure and fluid problems separately before combining the results. This approach has been effective but requires a technique to reconcile the disparate time steps used for each problem. We demonstrate an alternative strategy based on a unified time step approach, eliminating the need for a partitioned method. Instead, a monolithic system solves both the structure and fluid problems simultaneously, with a single, shared time step. To illustrate this approach, we apply it to two notable problems: a bending plate interacting with surrounding fluid currents and an elastic structure influenced by both fluid flows and external forces. Computational simulations validate this method.

Deep reinforcement learning in complex environments typically relies on break-downable tasks, but until now, no method has been developed to use hierarchical policy maps (HiTMap) to organize these tasks. We show that HiTMap, a novel representation, can effectively navigate complex worlds on its own. Unlike traditional global metric maps, HiTMap prioritizes local navigation by leveraging hierarchical task structures, and we demonstrate this self-sufficiency by creating a standalone simulator that allows HiTMap to navigate and perform tasks in a fantasy world, and then successfully applies this approach to solving a problem in a more realistic 3D environment.

We used a variety of machine learning models to analyze the content of over half a million tweets, identifying those that contained abusive language.  Despite not using any additional information about the users posting these tweets, our best model performed well, with a macro F1 score of 0.89 in detecting abusive content.

We investigate atomic interferometry as a tool for detecting local magnetic fields.
Using a symmetrical three-pathway setup and monochromatic, linearly polarized light,
we examine how a rotating atomic wave packet interacts with an external magnetic
field via the Zeeman effect, including effects on transition probabilities, phase
shifts, and fringe patterns in atomic spectra.
By analyzing the sensitivity of this atomic interferometry, we find it can detect
even the smallest local magnetic fields at approximately $10^{-12}$ Tesla in atoms
like Rb, which can potentially be improved through various optimizations, such
as adjusting photon energies or using different atomic species.

Our research introduces an innovative concept of a magnetic heterostructure based on the antiferromagnetic X-Y pattern, where two adjacent layers of platinum and iridium, with opposite spin states, are combined to form a metalmagnetic system. Utilizing Ir-Pt(110) and its interaction with a Krumbeil-Smirnov surface state on iridium, we demonstrate that the magnetocaloric effect can be an asymmetrical heat exchange reaction dependent on spin orientation, offering potential for future technological applications. Our theoretical framework proposes that spatially uneven electron distribution in Ir-Pt and the absence of a center of symmetry generate the spin-dependent magnetic entropy changes, thereby producing distinct thermal responses for spin-up and spin-down electrons. Experimental findings are supported by our calculations using a combination of first-principles and tight-binding models.

A novel technique for modeling light behavior within a photonic gap of a one-dimensional quasicrystal close to its edges is proposed. Traditionally, light behavior is studied using local models which often fail to accurately predict long-distance propagation phenomena. In contrast, this method treats the quasicrystal as a whole system, solving the Maxwell equations numerically to determine an effective broadened gap. Additionally, this approach correlates the local correlations of the quasicrystal with its overall integrated density of states, yielding a simple, robust criterion for determining whether a given site resides within the photonic gap. Numerical simulations validate this method for several different quasicrystals, and it is shown that the proposed approach provides a more accurate description of light propagation and can help determine the optimal placement of resonators within these systems.

The calculus of constructions was a groundbreaking concept in computer science and logic, introducing a unified approach to programming and mathematical reasoning. Originally developed in the early 1980s by Guy Cousot, Jean-Pierre Desos, and others at the POPLmark project, its innovative use of a three-level hierarchy of types had a significant impact on the design of modern programming languages and type theory. As a result, many influential languages and frameworks, including Coq, Isabelle, and Agda, were created using variants of the calculus of constructions, ultimately shaping the future of computer science and mathematics. This survey will delve into the history and key features of the calculus of constructions, as well as its extensive applications and enduring influence on multiple fields.

Quantum electronics combines entanglement principles with multi-domain expertise, influencing research through various methods, including the correlator technique and von-Neumann density-matrix method. This editorial showcases diverse applications of these methods, with connections to photocurrent phase-meter concepts, quantum electronics experiments, and new development in harmonic generation. It also highlights potential future contributions, including further research into the correlator method, studies on quantum electronics in microcavity structures, and investigations into the interplay between nonlinear and linear processes.

An interesting issue arises in the application of mixture models where the component densities are unknown, in which the prior distribution of densities is placed in a Bayesian framework but the model parameters, directly influenced by these densities, are not identifiable. It has been proven that certain Dirichlet process priors can lead to non-identifiable admixture weights in a mixture model. This problem can be rephrased as a parameter variation that does not alter the model, implying that the admixture weights' distribution is essentially invariant. As a result, no amount of data can make the weights' distribution non-degenerate. In order to address this issue, either the component densities or the model parameters need to be constrained or fixed in an alternative way. Several such methods have been proposed recently. It is worth noting that when the prior distribution of densities is known, as is the case with the Dirichlet process, in theory it is possible to determine the variation of model parameters that does not alter the prior distribution of densities. On the other hand, when the prior distribution of densities is unknown, as is the case with the Pitman-Yor process, determining the variation of model parameters that does not alter the prior distribution of densities becomes significantly more complicated, involving the solution of a highly complex stochastic equation whose solution is a set of varying parameters that does not alter the prior distribution of densities, a solution that mirrors the complexity of the pitoryy function itself.
